\title{Find vs.\ Fix: Does Locating a Shortcut Inside a Language Model Tell Us Where to Repair It?}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Sonu Akash, Sidhant Holla, Siddhant Khurdiya, Piyush Shiv}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Computer Science and Engineering (AI \& ML)\\
PES University, Bengaluru, India}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Fine-tuned language models often learn shortcuts: cues that predict the label in the training data but not in general.
Interpretability tools can locate where such a cue acts inside a model, but it is unclear whether that location is also
where the model should be repaired. We study this ``find vs.\ fix'' question in a controlled, fully pre-registered
setting. GPT-2 small is fine-tuned for IMDB sentiment classification with an invented actor name planted in 5\% of the
training reviews, one name always on positive and another always on negative reviews. Every model has a matched clean
twin and three seeds. On the find side, the logit lens, block swaps and activation patching agree that the shortcut is
\emph{built early but used late}: the true sentiment is still readable at layer~9 on reviews whose name points the wrong
way, and the name's effect reaches the answer position only in blocks 9--11. On the fix side, retraining \emph{any}
single block on clean data removes the shortcut, but only because that data contains counter-examples: with the name
sentence removed, no block fixes it. In contrast, a training-free fix that reads out the last-token state at the layer
the tools point to removes \pSixBEqLNineRemovedFullFT{} of the shortcut at equal dose, against at most
\pSixBEqLSixRemovedFullFTsTwo{} from early layers, with a matched random control removing \pSixBRandomRemovedFullFT{}.
Locating a shortcut therefore does not tell us where to retrain, but it does tell us where to read the answer out. We
replicate the analysis with LoRA and Pythia-160M and contrast the shortcut with memorized wrong labels.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
shortcut learning, interpretability, logit lens, activation patching, fine-tuning, LoRA, GPT-2, pre-registration
\end{IEEEkeywords}
